footerPosts.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
footerPosts.subtitle: Migrate your Spring Boot services from thread-pool exhaustion to JDK 21 virtual threads — the practical Spring developer guide
footerPosts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

footerPosts.title: ACID Properties Explained: How SQL Databases Guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
footerPosts.subtitle: A deep dive into PostgreSQL WAL logs, MVCC snapshot isolation, Write Skew anomalies, and crash recovery
footerPosts.brief: Trace how storage engines process high-stakes financial transactions like bank transfers using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC), and SSI locks without data loss or corruption.

footerPosts.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
footerPosts.subtitle: How modern NoSQL databases achieve atomicity and isolation without a single machine
footerPosts.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

footerPosts.subtitle: Is an LLM a brain in a jar? To make it truly useful, we need to give it access to the world. This guide explains RAG and Agents.
footerPosts.brief: Large Language Models are brilliant "brains in a jar." Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) hands them a constantly refreshed memory, while AI Agents give them tools to act in the world. Combined, they turn static knowledge into dynamic, goal-directed intelligence — the next frontier of practical AI.

footerPosts.brief: A single agent loop is enough for a demo, but production AI systems need explicit layers for routing, execution, memory, and evaluation. Those layers determine safety, latency, cost, and traceability far more than model choice alone.

footerPosts.title: AI Agents Explained: When LLMs Start Using Tools
footerPosts.subtitle: An LLM can talk, but an AI Agent can *act*. We explain how Agents use the ReAct framework to brow...
footerPosts.brief: A standard LLM is a brain in a jar — it can reason but cannot act. An **AI Agent** connects that brain to tools (web search, code execution, APIs). Instead of just answering a question, an agent executes a loop of Thought → Action → Observation until the goal is reached.

footerPosts.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
footerPosts.subtitle: A production-first guide to picking the right vector index for recall, latency, memory, and update patterns.
footerPosts.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

footerPosts.title: Apache Spark for Data Engineers: RDDs, DataFrames, and Structured Streaming

footerPosts.brief: Apache Spark distributes Python DataFrame jobs across a cluster of executors, using lazy evaluation and the Catalyst query optimizer to process terabytes with the same code that works on gigabytes. Master partitioning, shuffle-awareness, and Structured Streaming and you have a single engine for both batch and real-time pipelines.

footerPosts.title: Attention Mechanism Explained: How Transformers Learn to Focus
footerPosts.subtitle: From the query-key-value formulation to multi-head attention — the mechanism that made transformers dominate AI
footerPosts.brief: Attention lets every token in a sequence ask "what else is relevant to me?" — dynamically weighting relationships across all positions simultaneously. It replaced the fixed-size hidden-state bottleneck of RNNs and is the engine behind every GPT, BERT, ViT, and AlphaFold model you have ever used.

footerPosts.title: API Gateway vs. Load Balancer vs. Reverse Proxy: What's the Difference?
footerPosts.subtitle: They all sit in front of your servers. But do you need Nginx, HAProxy, or Kong? We clarify the roles of each component.
footerPosts.brief: A **Reverse Proxy** hides your servers and handles caching/SSL. A **Load Balancer** spreads traffic across server instances. An **API Gateway** manages API concerns — auth, rate limiting, routing, and protocol translation. Modern tools (Nginx, AWS ALB, Kong) often combine all three, but understanding what each layer does independently is essential for system design.

footerPosts.title: Backend for Frontend (BFF): Tailoring APIs for UI
footerPosts.subtitle: Mobile apps need less data than Desktop dashboards. Why serve them the same JSON? The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern solves this.
footerPosts.brief: A "one-size-fits-all" API causes bloated mobile payloads and underpowered desktop dashboards. The **Backend for Frontend (BFF)** pattern solves this by creating a dedicated API server for each client type — the mobile BFF reshapes data for small screens, the web BFF aggregates for dashboards.

footerPosts.title: BFS — Breadth-First Search: Level-by-Level Graph Exploration
footerPosts.subtitle: BFS explores graphs level by level using a queue — the key to shortest paths and level-order problems.
footerPosts.brief: BFS explores a graph level by level using a FIFO queue, guaranteeing the shortest path in unweighted graphs. Recognize BFS problems by keywords: "shortest path," "minimum steps," or "level order." Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V). Mark nodes visited on enqueue — never on dequeue.

footerPosts.title: Exploring Backtracking Techniques in Data Structures
footerPosts.subtitle: Backtracking is a brute-force algorithmic technique that solves problems by trying to build a sol...
footerPosts.brief: Backtracking is "Recursion with Undo." You try a path, explore it deeply, and if it fails, you **undo** your last decision and try the next option. It explores the full search space but prunes invalid branches early, making it far more efficient than brute force.

footerPosts.title: Big Data Architecture Patterns: Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh
footerPosts.subtitle: Choose ingestion, serving, and ownership patterns deliberately when data platforms start to scale.
footerPosts.brief: A serious data platform is defined less by where files are stored and more by how changes enter the system, how serving layers are materialized, and who owns quality over time. Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh are patterns for making those choices explicit.

footerPosts.title: Big Data 101: The 5 Vs, Ecosystem, and Why Scale Breaks Everything
footerPosts.subtitle: Why traditional databases fail at scale, what the 5 Vs really mean, and a practical map of the big data ecosystem from ingestion to insights.
footerPosts.brief: Traditional databases fail at big data scale for three concrete reasons — storage saturation, compute bottleneck, and write-lock contention. The 5 Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value) frame what makes data "big." A layered ecosystem — Kafka for ingestion, S3 for storage, Spark for processing, Snowflake for serving — assigns one tool per failure mode.

footerPosts.title: Exploring Different Types of Binary Trees
footerPosts.subtitle: Not all Binary Trees are created equal. We explain Full, Complete, Perfect, and Balanced Binary T...
footerPosts.brief: A Binary Tree has at most 2 children per node, but the **shape** of the tree determines performance. A **Full** tree has 0 or 2 children. A **Complete** tree fills left-to-right. A **Perfect** tree is a symmetric triangle. A **Degenerate** tree becomes a linked list with $O(N)$ search.

footerPosts.title: Big O Notation Explained: Time Complexity, Space Complexity, and Why They Matter in Interviews
footerPosts.subtitle: Master Big O notation: measure algorithm efficiency from O(1) to O(n²) with growth diagrams, worked examples, and the interview mental model.
footerPosts.brief: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's resource usage *grows* as input size grows — not how fast it runs on your laptop. Learn to identify the 7 complexity classes (O(1) through O(n!)), derive time and space complexity by counting loops and stack frames, and communicate your analysis in three sentences that satisfy any FAANG interviewer.

footerPosts.title: Binary Search Patterns: Five Variants Every Senior Engineer Knows
footerPosts.subtitle: Binary search has five distinct patterns — classic, leftmost, rightmost, rotated arrays, and 2D matrices.
footerPosts.brief: Binary search has five patterns beyond the classic "find the target": leftmost position, rightmost position, rotated array search, minimum in rotated array, and 2D matrix search. The root of every off-by-one bug is a mismatched loop condition and boundary update. Learn the invariant for each pattern and you will never write a broken binary search again.

articles.title: System Design Message Queues and Event-Driven Architecture: Building Reliable Asynchronous Systems
articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

Message queues and event-driven architecture let services communicate asynchronously, absorb bursty traffic, and isolate failures. The core design challenge is not adding a queue — it is defining delivery semantics, retry behavior, and idempotent consumers.






Queues are not a default replacement for APIs. They are a pressure-relief boundary when synchronous chains become fragile under burst traffic or partial ou…

This walkthrough focuses on **When to Use Event-Driven Queues and When Not To**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- When to use - Work is naturally asynchronous: notifications, enrichment, indexing, billing reconciliation.
- - Producer traffic is bursty, but outcomes can be delayed by seconds or minutes.
- - You need durable handoff between independently scaled services.

**Concepts in play:** message-queues, stack-and-queue-data-structures, event-driven-architecture, consistency-replication

## Stage 1 — How the Pattern Works: Producer, Broker, Consumer, Recovery

- The practical flow is simple to explain and strict to implement.
- Producer publishes an event with stable schema and idempotency key.
- Broker persists and routes events by topic/partition.
- Consumer processes event side effects.

*Applies **message-queues** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Consumer processes event side effects.

## Stage 2 — Deep Dive: Internals That Make or Break Async Reliability

- Internals: Ordering, Acknowledgment, and Schema Evolution Ordering is partition-scoped, not global.
- If one business entity needs strict order, all events for that entity must land on the same partition key.
- Acknowledgment strategy determines correctness: 1.
- If you ack before step 3, crashes can lose work.

*Applies **stack-and-queue-data-structures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** If you ack before step 3, crashes can lose work.

## Stage 3 — Event Pipeline Flow: Publish, Process, Retry, and Recover

- This is the minimum viable reliability loop.
- If any node is missing, incident load shifts to manual cleanup.
- Every path ends in a safe ack or DLQ route — there is no silent discard.
- 📊 Pub-Sub: Publisher to Subscribers This pub-sub sequence diagram shows how a single OrderCreated event published to a topic fans out simultaneously to two independent subscriber services, each of which processes the e…

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

```mermaid



flowchart TD
    A[Producer validates and publishes event] --> B[Broker topic partition]
    B --> C[Consumer reads event]
    C --> D{Idempotency key already processed?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Ack and skip duplicate]
    D -->|No| F[Execute side effect]
    F --> G{Success?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Record dedupe key then ack]
    G -->|No| I[Retry with backoff]
    I --> J{Retry limit reached?}
    J -->|No| C
    J -->|Yes| K[Route to DLQ and alert owner]

```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Publisher
    participant T as Topic
    participant S1 as EmailService
    participant S2 as InventoryService
    P->>T: Publish OrderCreated event
    T->>S1: Deliver to EmailService
    T->>S2: Deliver to InventoryService
    S1-->>T: Ack
    S2-->>T: Ack

```

**Observable outcome:** 📊 Pub-Sub: Publisher to Subscribers This pub-sub sequence diagram shows how a single OrderCreated event published to a topic fans out simultaneously to two independent subscriber services, each of which processes the e…

## Stage 4 — Real-World Applications: Flash-Sale Checkout Under Hard Constraints

- Scenario constraints: - 70k checkouts/minute during a 10-minute flash sale.
- - Payment provider has 2% transient timeout rate.
- - Inventory updates must be per-item ordered.
- - Duplicate charge rate must remain under 0.01%.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Duplicate charge rate must remain under 0.01%.

## Stage 5 — Lessons From Running Async Systems in Production

- - Queue adoption is only successful when correctness rules are explicit before the first message is sent.
- - Idempotent consumers are mandatory for at-least-once delivery — not optional.
- - Partition strategy is a business decision, not only a scaling decision.
- Order guarantees map to business entities.

*Applies **message-queues** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Order guarantees map to business entities.

## End-to-end outcome

When to use - Work is naturally asynchronous: notifications, enrichment, indexing, billing reconciliation.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: Queues vs Synchronous Calls in Architecture Reviews

The retry and dead-letter semantics in AMQP are expressed through the acknowledgment itself.


## Failure and degraded modes

### When to use

- **Detection:** - Work is naturally asynchronous: notifications, enrichment, indexing, billing reconciliation.
- **User or operator impact:** - Work is naturally asynchronous: notifications, enrichment, indexing, billing reconciliation.

### When not to use

- **Detection:** - A user-facing action needs immediate, deterministic completion.
- **User or operator impact:** - A user-facing action needs immediate, deterministic completion.

articles.title: CQRS Pattern: Separating Write Models from Query Models at Scale
articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

CQRS works when read and write workloads diverge, but only with explicit freshness budgets and projection reliability. The hard part is not separating models — it is operating lag, replay, and rollback safely.



```architecture
{
  "ok": true,
  "diagram": {
    "version": 1,
    "title": "CQRS Pattern: Separating Read and Write Models",
    "description": "This architecture illustrates the CQRS pattern, separating…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why CQRS Exists: Protect Write Truth While Shaping Fast Reads**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Teams usually reach for CQRS after the same failure pattern repeats: one transactional model is asked to serve invariants, dashboards, search, timelines, and external API reads all at once.
- The result is often lock contention on the write path, expensive joins on the read path, and emergency cache layers that hide freshness problems instead of fixing them.
- In architecture reviews, CQRS should answer four operational questions before anyone sketches a read model: - Which business rules must stay synchronous on the write path?

**Concepts in play:** event-driven-architecture, api-gateway, caching, transaction-isolation-distributed-acid

## Stage 1 — The Boundary Model: Command Side, Event Stream, Projection Side

- At a practical level, CQRS is not just two databases.
- It is a contract about where truth is written and how derivative views are built.
- 📊 Command-Query Split: Write Side vs Read Side This flowchart draws the CQRS architectural boundary in its simplest form: commands flow through a handler to a write store, and a projection worker asynchronously propaga…
- The critical visual detail is that the outbox or CDC mechanism sits at the boundary between the write and read subgraphs, making the write-to-read propagation explicit and decoupled.

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Write Side
    CMD[Command] --> CH[Command Handler]
    CH --> WDB[(Write Store)]
    WDB --> OBX[Outbox / CDC]
  end
  subgraph Read Side
    OBX --> PW[Projection Worker]
    PW --> RDB[(Query Store)]
    RDB --> QH[Query Handler]
    QH --> QRY[Query Response]
  end
```

**Observable outcome:** The critical visual detail is that the outbox or CDC mechanism sits at the boundary between the write and read subgraphs, making the write-to-read propagation explicit and decoupled.

## Stage 2 — How the Write Path and Read Path Stay Separate

- A healthy CQRS flow looks boring on purpose: 1.
- The command handler validates the requested state change against current write-side rules.
- The transaction commits the write and records an outbox event or change record in the same durability boundary.
- A relay publishes that committed event to projection workers.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant CA as Command API
  participant CH as Command Handler
  participant WS as Write Store
  participant OB as Outbox
  participant PW as Projection Worker
  C->>CA: POST /orders (command)
  CA->>CH: validate and handle
  CH->>WS: commit to write store
  WS->>OB: record outbox event (atomic)
  OB->>PW: relay committed event
  PW->>PW: update read model with checkpoint
  CA-->>C: 202 Accepted
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant QA as Query API
  participant RM as Read Model
  participant QS as Query Store
  C->>QA: GET /orders/timeline
  QA->>RM: query read model
  RM->>QS: fetch from query store
  QS-->>RM: projection data
  RM-->>QA: shaped response
  QA-->>C: timeline response (may lag write by seconds)
```

**Observable outcome:** A relay publishes that committed event to projection workers.

## Stage 3 — Deep Dive: Lag, Replay, and Projection Safety

- The Internals: Write Authority, Checkpoints, and Read Staleness The write side is the only place where business invariants should be enforced.
- Projection workers are downstream materializers; they should never be asked to resolve conflicts that belong to the command model.
- A replayed projection should rebuild a view from committed events, not guess what the latest truth is.
- Operators usually need three durable markers: - a source-of-truth commit version or event ID, - a per-projection checkpoint, - a freshness budget that maps lag into user impact.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Operators usually need three durable markers: - a source-of-truth commit version or event ID, - a per-projection checkpoint, - a freshness budget that maps lag into user impact.

## Stage 4 — Operator Field Note: Freshness Budgets Fail Before Correctness Does

- In incident reviews, the first visible symptom of CQRS trouble is usually outdated reads, not corrupted writes.
- Support tickets say a status is old long before anyone proves the write path is wrong.
- Operators usually find that the most valuable architecture review artifact is a freshness table per read surface: acceptable lag, pager threshold, and replay procedure.

*Applies **transaction-isolation-distributed-acid** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Operators usually find that the most valuable architecture review artifact is a freshness table per read surface: acceptable lag, pager threshold, and replay procedure.

## Stage 5 — CQRS Flow: Commit Once, Project Many

- This flowchart shows the full CQRS data pipeline from a single command API entry point through transactional write, outbox relay, and projection worker to multiple specialized query stores.
- Two additional outputs — a committed version token returned to the read path and a projection checkpoint — make the consistency and replay properties of the pipeline explicit.
- The key takeaway is that a single committed write fans out to as many read models as the system needs, each optimized independently, all derived from the same immutable source of truth in the write store.

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Command API] --> B[Validate business rule]
  B --> C[Transactional write store]
  C --> D[Outbox or change stream]
  D --> E[Projection worker]
  E --> F[Query store]
  F --> G[API or UI read path]
  E --> H[Projection checkpoint]
  C --> I[Committed version token]
  I --> G
```

**Observable outcome:** The key takeaway is that a single committed write fans out to as many read models as the system needs, each optimized independently, all derived from the same immutable source of truth in the write store.

## Stage 6 — Practical Example: Order Service With Axon Framework

- The order scenario from the previous section maps directly to Axon's programming model.
- Commands flow in through CommandGateway , the aggregate persists events to the event store, and the projection worker builds the timeline read model asynchronously.
- Maven dependency Commands and queries as plain records Commands carry intent; queries carry selection criteria.
- Write side: aggregate enforces invariants, never touches the read store AggregateLifecycle.apply() commits the event to the Axon event store.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[REST POST /orders] --> B[CommandGateway]
  B --> C[OrderAggregate]
  C --> D[EventStore]
  D --> E[EventBus]
  E --> F[@EventHandler Projection Worker]
  F --> G[QueryStore]
  G --> H[QueryGateway]
  H --> I[REST GET /timeline]
```

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.axonframework</groupId>
  <artifactId>axon-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
  <version>4.9.3</version>
</dependency>
```

**Observable outcome:** Write side: aggregate enforces invariants, never touches the read store AggregateLifecycle.apply() commits the event to the Axon event store.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- - CQRS is a control boundary between write truth and read convenience, not a blanket microservices rule.
- - Freshness budgets and replay tooling matter as much as the schema design.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: When CQRS Earns Its Complexity

Start with one domain that already hurts, such as orders or billing, and prove that lag, replay, and recovery are manageable before expanding the pattern elsewhere.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Trade-offs and Failure Modes

- **Detection:** CQRS is worth the cost when read workloads are truly different.
- **User or operator impact:** CQRS is worth the cost when read workloads are truly different.

articles.title: Event Sourcing Pattern: Auditability, Replay, and Evolution of Domain State
articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

Event sourcing pays off when regulatory audit history and replay are first-class requirements — but it demands strict schema evolution, a snapshot strategy, and a framework that owns aggregate lifecycle. Spring Boot + Axon Framework is the fastest production-grade path on the JVM.

In 2017, a GitLab database administrator ran `rm -rf` on the wrong production server. They had no event log — just nightly snapshots. Si…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why Storing Events Instead of State Changes Everything**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- In 2017, a GitLab database administrator ran rm -rf on the wrong production server.
- They had no event log — just nightly snapshots.
- Six hours of user data was lost permanently, and thousands of repositories were irrecoverable.

**Concepts in play:** event-driven-architecture, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, consistency-replication, design-principles-solid

## Stage 1 — The Four Building Blocks of an Event-Sourced System

- Every production event-sourced system has four roles: 1.
- Command — an intent to change state; validated against current aggregate state before writing.
- Aggregate — the consistency boundary; enforces invariants, emits events, and advances its internal state machine.
- Event Store — the append-only log; events are immutable, each aggregate instance owns a stream by ID.

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Event Store — the append-only log; events are immutable, each aggregate instance owns a stream by ID.

## Stage 2 — How a Command Flows into an Auditable Event Stream

- Solid arrows show the live command path.
- Dashed arrows show replay — the TrackingEventProcessor resets its token to reconstruct the query model for audit at any historical timestamp.
- The aggregate never writes directly to the query model.
- It emits events; projections consume them independently.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C[Client Command] --> CH["Command Handler (SubscriptionAggregate)"]
    CH -->|"validates invariants applies event"| ES[(Event Store Append-Only Log)]
    ES -->|"event published on event bus"| P["BillingHistoryProjection (Event Handler)"]
    P --> QM[(Query Model BillingHistoryRepository)]
    QM -->|"query response"| Q[GetBillingHistoryQuery]

    ES -. "token-based replay" .-> RP["Replay Processor (TrackingEventProcessor)"]
    RP -. "rebuilds view for audit dispute" .-> QM

    style ES fill:#f5f5f5,stroke:#555
    style QM fill:#e8f4e8,stroke:#555
    style RP fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#f90,stroke-dasharray: 5 5
```

**Observable outcome:** It emits events; projections consume them independently.

## Stage 3 — Deep Dive: Inside the Aggregate: State Machines, Snapshots, and Schema Evolution

- Internals: Aggregate State Reconstruction An aggregate's state exists only in memory during command processing.
- Before handling a command, the framework loads the aggregate by replaying every past event for that aggregate ID in sequence.
- Each @EventSourcingHandler method advances internal state — status flags, counters, IDs — until the aggregate is fully current.
- The command handler then checks invariants against that reconstructed in-memory state.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The command handler then checks invariants against that reconstructed in-memory state.

## Stage 4 — Axon Framework and EventStoreDB: Event Sourcing on the JVM

- Axon Framework is a Spring Boot-native Java framework that manages the full event-sourcing lifecycle: aggregate command handling, event persistence, snapshotting, replay, upcasting, and projection tracking.
- EventStoreDB is a purpose-built append-only database with server-side projections and persistent subscription support — the recommended backend for production Axon deployments requiring audit-grade storage.
- These tools solve the event-sourcing problem by owning the infrastructure that makes aggregates deterministic: Axon's @CommandHandler / @EventSourcingHandler pattern enforces the strict separation between command valida…
- Teams write domain logic; Axon owns the replay machinery.

*Applies **design-principles-solid** to the decision above.*

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.axonframework</groupId>
  <artifactId>axon-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
  <version>4.9.3</version>
</dependency>
<!-- Optional: EventStoreDB connector replaces the default JPA event store -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.axonframework.extensions.eventstored</groupId>
  <artifactId>axon-eventstoredb-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
</dependency>
```

**Observable outcome:** Teams write domain logic; Axon owns the replay machinery.

## Stage 5 — Real-World Applications

- Event sourcing earns its complexity where audit trails and replay are first-class business requirements.

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

## Stage 6 — Subscription Billing: Building the Aggregate, Projection, and Replay

- Scenario: A billing platform tracks the lifecycle of each subscription — CREATED → ACTIVATED → SUSPENDED → CANCELLED .
- Every state transition is an immutable domain event appended to the subscription's event stream.
- When a customer disputes a charge, the support team replays the event stream to reconstruct exactly what the account looked like at the moment of the disputed transaction.
- Maven Dependency Domain Events (Immutable Value Objects) Each event is a value object with no setters.
